title: My dialogue is going to be determined by the questions that I ask
header_line: My analysis of one book on an entrepreneur's life. Not a summary of the book. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.

lines.text: If you sat across from someone who sees the world very differently from you, what would you ask first?

I said the author gave his son a choice, as he retells the book: go to one capital city or another. He was throwing him into a pretty extreme experience. He is just like his father. He is making him adapt.
I said the son is already learning from his father: I'm just going to go with an open mind. Let's get everybody together. Let's open a dialogue.

I set an exercise. Imagine you are sitting at a table with the leaders of a country in deep conflict with yours. You are there for a social meeting. Maybe you have an agenda. Maybe you don't. What would be your attitude?

A student said: I would try to be as peaceful as possible, to gain their perspective, so I understood where they were coming from. I said: how much we have to gain by being good listeners and suspending judgment.

What question would you ask? A student said: what is their motivation for their feelings, and what do they perceive the problem to actually be, because it is usually different from what we think the problem is.

I asked: if you have that kind of opportunity, are you going to freeze, or take the opportunity to learn? You don't want to be the person who is quiet. You want to be inquisitive, asking questions, growing empathy between the two sides.

groups.heading: My dialogue is going to be determined by the questions that I ask

lines.text: Does this help in business, I asked? A student said: you are learning more about the person you are talking to, even if you are just doing business with someone. I said: you need to learn who they are.

Are you going to let political opinions affect the way you perceive another person and the way you can do business together? Should your view block you from absorbing the opinion of the other side? Should it block you from listening? No.

When I'm in these situations, I said, I have to suspend judgment. I have to listen. I have to be almost like a journalist, and develop really good questions. My dialogue is going to be determined by the questions that I ask. Those questions aren't going to be charged. They aren't going to be judgmental. They are going to be open.

A student told of a family member who was asked, in a tense moment, to be the bridge between two sides. I said: it is not about the language. It is about understanding, suspending judgment, and being able to have the responsibility of carrying the message without contaminating the message.
My tip for a dense chapter: look up the timeline first. Write down on a piece of paper what happened when. That will be very helpful before you read.
What open question would you ask someone you disagree with?

exercise.title: Five minutes
steps: Write someone you disagree with, in your work or life.
Write what they might perceive the problem to be.
Write three open, uncharged questions you would ask them.
Write how you will suspend judgment in the first five minutes.
Write one dense thing you have to read: write its timeline first.

check.q: What did I say his dialogue is determined by?
What kind of questions did I say to ask?
What did I say is not about the language when you are a bridge between two sides?
choices: Understanding, suspending judgment and carrying the message

recap: Ask open questions. Suspend judgment and listen.
